7 Diet and growth

7.1 Nutrients

Key words: anaemia · carbohydrate · fat · minerals · nutrients · oil · protein · starch · vitamin A · vitamin C · vitamin D · vitamins

Nutrients are substances found in food that you need in order to stay healthy. There are six kinds of nutrient: carbohydrate, protein, fat, vitamins, minerals and water.

Carbohydrates, fats and proteins

Carbohydrates give you energy. Rice contains a lot of starch, which is a type of carbohydrate. After you eat starch, the body breaks it down into a sugar called glucose. Glucose is the fuel that your cells use for respiration, to release energy.

Protein is needed for making new cells. So you need protein to grow, and to repair the body if it is damaged. Protein is also needed to make haemoglobin and antibodies. Chicken and beans contain a lot of protein.

Fats and oils also give you energy, and they are needed to make cell membranes. Fats and oils are very similar, but fats are solid at normal temperatures and oils are liquid. Avocado contains fats and oils.

NutrientGood sourcesWhy the body needs it
Carbohydraterice, bread, pasta, potatoes, sugarreleases energy in respiration
Proteinmeat, fish, eggs, beans, pulses, dairygrowth and repair; haemoglobin and antibodies
Fat and oilavocado, nuts, oils, butterenergy store, cell membranes, heat insulation

Energy stores

You do not eat all the time, but you need energy all the time. You get almost all of your energy from the carbohydrates and fats that you eat. You can also get energy from protein if you run out of carbohydrates and fats.

  • A short-term store: a small amount of carbohydrate is stored in your cells, especially in the liver and muscles.
  • A long-term store: fat is stored in special cells underneath the skin and around some of the body organs.

Fat stores under the skin also work as heat insulation.

Remember: you can test a food for starch with iodine solution. Iodine solution is orange-brown, and turns very dark blue-black when it mixes with starch.

Vitamins

Vitamins are nutrients that are needed in only small amounts, but if you do not eat them you can become ill. Each kind of vitamin is given a letter.

Vitamin A helps your eyes to work well, and is especially important for seeing when it is quite dark. People who do not get enough vitamin A may not be able to see anything at night. Vitamin A also helps your white blood cells to fight pathogens. Good sources are green vegetables, carrots, squash, fruit, foods made from milk, and some kinds of fish.

Vitamin C helps the skin to stay strong and to heal quickly, and keeps blood vessels and bones healthy. Too little vitamin C causes scurvy: the person feels weak and may have swollen, bleeding gums. Good sources are fresh fruit and vegetables — citrus fruits especially, but also potatoes and colourful berries.

Vitamin D is needed for strong bones and teeth, because it helps the body to absorb calcium from food. Oily fish is the best food source, but most of your vitamin D is made in your own skin when sunlight falls onto it. Too little vitamin D in children stops their bones growing normally; this illness is called rickets.

Minerals

Minerals are nutrients needed in small amounts. Two of the most important are calcium and iron.

Calcium is found in bones and teeth, so you need plenty of it to make them strong. Foods made from milk are excellent sources. Seeds and some types of nut, such as almonds, also contain a lot of calcium.

Iron is needed to make haemoglobin. Without enough iron you cannot make enough haemoglobin, so not enough oxygen is transported around the body. This causes anaemia, which makes a person feel very tired. Good sources of iron are red meat, dark green vegetables, many kinds of fish and shellfish, and some nuts and seeds.

Water

Water is the sixth nutrient. Almost 90 % of a person's body weight is water. Water inside cells lets all the different chemicals dissolve so that they can react together, and these reactions keep you alive. Water in the blood lets the blood flow easily, so that substances can be transported all over the body.

7.2 A balanced diet

Key words: balanced diet · constipation · fibre

Diet

Your diet is the food that you eat each day. A balanced diet is one that provides all the different kinds of nutrient, and the right amount of energy.

How much energy?

Different people need different amounts of energy each day.

  • Someone who does a lot of exercise, or has an active job, needs more energy.
  • Someone who sits down for most of the day needs less energy.
  • A person who is still growing needs extra energy, because energy is needed to make cells divide.
  • Tall people usually need more energy than small people.

Different diets

Everyone needs plenty of minerals and vitamins, but people vary in how much protein and carbohydrate they need.

Young people who are still growing need a lot of protein to make new cells, enough carbohydrate for the energy they use, and a little fat for energy and for making the membranes of the new cells.

People who sit down for a lot of the day do not use up as much energy, so they do not need to eat as much carbohydrate or fat as someone who moves around all day or does a lot of sport.

A pregnant woman needs plenty of protein to build her baby's new cells, lots of iron to make haemoglobin for her own blood and her baby's blood, and plenty of calcium for building her baby's bones.

Fibre

You also need to eat plenty of fibre. Fibre is not actually a nutrient, because you cannot digest it — it does not go into the blood or to your cells. Instead it travels all the way through the digestive system and leaves the body in the faeces.

Fibre is still very important. It keeps the digestive system healthy and helps to prevent constipation, when the digestive system slows down and faeces collect inside it instead of being passed out.

Fibre is mostly cellulose. Plant cell walls are made of cellulose, so foods made from plants are good sources: cereal grains, seeds, and fresh fruit and vegetables. These foods usually contain lots of different minerals and vitamins as well.

Food groups

It can be difficult to think about which nutrients are in each kind of food. The food triangle makes this easier. The bigger the area in the triangle, the greater the proportion of your diet that kind of food should make up.

Position in the triangleFoodsWhat they provide
Bottom (largest)rice, bread, pasta — preferably whole grainstarch and fibre
Nextfresh fruit and vegetablesminerals, vitamins and fibre
Nextmeat, fish, eggs, pulses, dairy productsprotein
Top (smallest)sweets and fried foodseat only a little

Not too much

Some things should not be eaten in large amounts.

  • Too much sugar can make your teeth decay, and increases the risk of an illness called diabetes.
  • Too much fat, oil or carbohydrate can make you put on weight, which puts a strain on your joints, heart and other body organs.
  • Too much animal fat increases the risk of developing heart disease.
Remember: a balanced diet is not just "enough food". It must contain every kind of nutrient, in roughly the right proportions, and supply the right amount of energy for that particular person.

7.3 Growth, development and health

Key words: carbon monoxide · development · embryo · nicotine · particulates · tar

Growth

Every person on Earth began life as a single cell. That cell divided to produce two cells; each of those cells grew, then divided again. Growth happens by this repeated pattern: cells divide, then the new cells grow.

At first all the cells are the same. They form a little ball of cells called an embryo, and eventually a baby. This all happens inside the mother's body. A baby continues to grow until it is about 18–20 years old.

Cells contain a lot of protein, and energy is needed to make cells divide. That is why a pregnant woman and a growing child need plenty of protein in their diet, as well as enough energy.

Development

Becoming an adult involves more than just getting bigger. As the embryo grows into a baby, all its different tissues and organs are formed. As the baby grows into a child, its leg muscles and bones become stronger so that it can walk and then run, and its brain develops as it learns to talk and to play.

These changes are called development. Everyone grows and develops at different rates, but everyone goes through the same stages: baby, toddler, child, adolescent, adult. Each stage blends gradually into the next one — there are no sharp divisions between them.

Remember: growth means getting bigger; development means becoming more complex and gaining new abilities.

Exercise and health

Taking regular exercise:

  • uses up some of the energy in the food you eat, so less is stored as fat
  • makes the heart and muscles work hard, so they become strong
  • can make people feel more cheerful and positive about life.

Smoking

Smoking cigarettes damages the smoker's health. It also damages the health of people around them, who accidentally breathe in the smoke. Tobacco contains many different harmful substances.

SubstanceWhat it does
Nicotineaddictive, so smokers find it very difficult to stop; narrows blood vessels so blood cannot get through easily, increasing the risk of heart disease
Tara mixture of dark, sticky substances; some of its chemicals cause cancer, including lung cancer
Carbon monoxidea poisonous gas that combines with haemoglobin, so the blood carries less oxygen and cells cannot release enough energy by respiration
Particulatestiny particles of carbon and other materials that get trapped in the lungs and break down the walls of the alveoli, leaving big spaces instead of millions of tiny alveoli

Cancer happens when cells start dividing out of control and spread to other parts of the body.

7.4 Moving the body

Key words: antagonistic muscles · ball-and-socket joints · biceps · contraction · exoskeleton · hinge joints · joints · muscles · relax · skeleton · tendons · triceps

The skeleton

Animals' bodies are supported by a skeleton. Insects and other arthropods have their skeleton on the outside of the body; this is called an exoskeleton. Your skeleton is inside your body and is made of bones.

Bones are hard and strong, and contain a lot of calcium. If you do not have enough calcium in your diet, your bones may not grow properly. Bones also contain living cells, so you need protein in the diet to build strong bones.

Joints

Bones cannot bend. Movement in the skeleton can only take place where two bones meet one another. These places are called joints.

  • Hinge joints work like the hinges on a door. They let the bones move back and forth in one direction only — for example the elbow, the knee and the joints in the fingers.
  • Ball-and-socket joints let the bones move in a complete circle. One bone has an end shaped like a ball, and the other has a cup, or socket, that the ball fits into — for example the shoulder and the hip.

Joints in the arm

The arm contains the shoulder joint, the elbow joint, the wrist joint and all the joints in the fingers.

JointTypeBones that meet
Shoulderball-and-socketscapula and humerus
Elbowhingehumerus, radius and ulna
Finger jointshingefinger bones

Muscles

Bones and joints cannot move themselves. You use muscles to move bones at joints.

Muscles are made of specialised cells that are able to make themselves shorter. This is called contraction. Muscles use energy to contract, and they get that energy from glucose by respiration. The more your muscles contract, the more glucose they use.

Muscles can produce a strong pulling force when they contract. Many muscles are attached to bones by tough cords called tendons. When the muscle contracts it pulls on the tendon, which pulls on the bone, and the bone moves at a joint.

The biceps is the bigger muscle in the diagram. 'Bi-' means two: the biceps is named after the two tendons that attach it to the scapula. Its other end is attached to the radius.

The triceps is the longer, thinner muscle. 'Tri-' means three, and the triceps has three tendons. It is attached to the scapula and the humerus at one end, and to the ulna at the other.

Remember: tendons are not stretchy. If they stretched, the pull of the muscle would not be passed on to the bone.

Bending and straightening the elbow

To bend the arm, the biceps contracts and the triceps relaxes. Your brain sends an electrical impulse along a neurone to the biceps. The muscle cells respond by contracting, so the whole muscle gets shorter. The contracting biceps pulls on its tendon, so the radius moves upwards and the elbow bends.

Muscles can only pull — they cannot push. A muscle can produce a force by contracting, but not by getting longer. So the biceps cannot push the arm straight again; another muscle is needed to pull it straight.

To straighten the arm, the triceps contracts and the biceps relaxes. The contracting triceps pulls on its tendon, so the ulna moves downwards.

Antagonistic muscles

The biceps and the triceps work as a team.

  • To bend the arm, the biceps contracts and the triceps relaxes.
  • To straighten the arm, the triceps contracts and the biceps relaxes.

Two muscles that work together like this are called antagonistic muscles. When one of them contracts it moves the bones at a joint in one direction; when the other contracts it moves them back the other way.

In a model arm, a piece of wood represents the humerus and another represents the radius, joined by a freely moving pivot at the 'elbow'. A newton meter attached to hooks at different distances from the pivot represents the biceps. The further the newton meter is from the elbow, the smaller the force needed to hold the 'radius' horizontal — because the turning effect of a force depends on its distance from the pivot.

Summary checklist

  • I can name the six nutrients and say why the body needs each of them.
  • I can name good food sources of protein, carbohydrate, fat, vitamin A, vitamin C, vitamin D, calcium and iron.
  • I can describe the illnesses caused by a lack of vitamin C, vitamin D and iron.
  • I can explain what is meant by a balanced diet.
  • I can explain why different people need different diets.
  • I can explain why fibre is important even though it is not a nutrient.
  • I can explain why no one should eat too much sugar or fat.
  • I can describe how organisms grow.
  • I can explain what is meant by development.
  • I can explain why exercise is good for a person's health.
  • I can explain how nicotine, tar, carbon monoxide and particulates damage health.
  • I can name the bones in the arm.
  • I can identify some hinge joints and ball-and-socket joints in the body.
  • I can describe how muscles produce a force when they contract.
  • I can explain how the biceps and triceps work as antagonistic muscles to move the arm at the elbow.
